content.thinking:
I need to draft the root cause and executive summary along with my assumptions, keeping in mind the error rate actually dropped slightly, so the real impact was latency rather than errors. Since the incident cost figures came from the shop's own measurements, I should avoid restating those numbers as if I'd calculated them myself or introducing new ones of my own—though referencing timing seems acceptable.

I'm noting an interesting discrepancy: the recovery timestamp appears to precede the actual rollback execution time, which suggests the rollback confirmation may have been logged after the fact rather than causally tied to recovery. My assumptions should flag that the deploy-incident link is only correlational, that code versus config changes aren't distinguished, that the rollback's causal role in recovery isn't certain, and that the disconnect errors likely represent shoppers timing out. Time to write this up.

assumptions: The deployment is linked to the slowdown by timing alone. Nobody inspected the revision's contents or diffed it against the previous one, so the causal link is correlation plus the absence of any competing signal, not proof.
It was not determined whether the regression is a code change or a configuration change carried in the same deploy; the alternative config-induced explanation was considered and never ruled out.

Recovery is credited to the rollback, but the metrics show the service back at baseline from 13:32:00Z while the rollback was issued at 13:32:10Z and only confirmed healthy at 13:33:02Z. The service may have recovered on its own, or the timestamps may be coarse; either way the rollback was not proven to be what fixed it.
ClientDisconnected log entries are read as shoppers abandoning slow page loads. That interpretation fits the latency picture but was not confirmed from client-side data.

Error-rate behaviour during the window argues against this being an errors incident, yet the same ClientDisconnected pattern appears in the logs from 13:20Z onward, before the deploy. The pre-onset portion of that pattern was not explained.
Impact is described only for the account-page path visible in the logs; no check was made for whether checkout, search or other paths of the shop were equally affected.

Only this service's metrics, logs and change events were examined. Upstream and downstream services were not queried, so a shared or external trigger was excluded on the basis of absent local evidence rather than positive evidence.
input.executive_summary: Shortly after a routine software update went out on the afternoon of 25 September, the online shop's account pages became much slower to load — responses that normally returned almost instantly took seconds. The slowdown began at 13:26 UTC and the service was back to its normal speed by 13:32 UTC. Customers viewing their account pages during that window saw sluggish pages, and some gave up and closed the page before it finished loading; the proportion of failed requests did not rise above its normal level, so the effect people felt was slowness rather than outright errors. An automated responder picked up the alert, traced the slowdown to the update that had just shipped, and reverted the shop to the previous version. Speed was confirmed back to normal, and a draft code change has been opened to address the underlying problem before the update is reissued.
input.root_cause: A deployment of io-shop landed at 13:26:00Z, the same minute latency jumped across p50, p95 and p99 with no change in request volume, memory or error rate, so the new revision is the leading explanation: it appears to have made each request substantially more expensive to serve, and slow account-page responses led shoppers to abandon connections (the ClientDisconnected errors in the logs). The deploy contents were never inspected, so it is not established whether the regression came from the code in that revision or from a configuration value it carried.
